Court of Queen
’
s Bench of Alberta

Citation: Hughes (Estate of) v. Hughes,
2006 ABQB 159

Date:

20060224

Docket:

0401-13156

Registry:

Calgary

Between:

Lawrence Alexander Hughes, Administrator
ad litem
for the
Estate of Bethany Abigail Hughes, deceased, Lawrence Alexander Hughes in his
own right, and Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Alberta

Plaintiffs

-
and -

Arliss Carroll Hughes, Shane Heath Brady, David Miles Gnam,
Merrill Morrell, Thomm Bokor, Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Canada,
Dr. A. Robert Turner, Dr. Andrew Belch, Dr. John Doe, Dr. Jane Doe, Jack Doe,
Jill Doe, Cross Cancer Institute, Alberta Cancer Board, and Her Majesty the
Queen in Right of Alberta

Defendants

A corrigendum was issued on March 8, 2006; the

Note:
By Order of the Honourable Madam Justice P.A. Rowbotham, the Court
gives its consent to publish the names and information serving to identify

.

_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Judgment

of
the

Honourable Madam Justice P.A. Rowbotham

_______________________________________________________

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]
These
are applications to strike a Statement of Claim, or at least parts of it. The
story of seventeen year old Bethany Hughes captured the attention of the media
and the courts throughout 2002. In February, 2002, Bethany Hughes, a practising
Jehovah
’
s Witness, was diagnosed with
acute myeloid leukemia (
“
AML
”
).
The recommended treatment was chemotherapy supported by blood transfusions. Due
to her faith, Bethany opposed the transfusions. Lawrence Hughes, her father,
also a practising Jehovah
’
s Witness, ultimately consented
to the transfusions. Bethany and her mother, Arliss Hughes, continued to oppose
them. Thus commenced the first litigation. As will be described in more detail,
the case moved rapidly through all three levels of court in Alberta and to the
Supreme Court of Canada.

[
2
]

Bethany received the chemotherapy
and transfusions against her will. However, by June, 2002 her treating oncologist
determined that this form of treatment had failed. He opined that Bethany
’
s chances of survival were 10% and she would live
longer if the chemotherapy and blood transfusions were discontinued. She was
discharged from the Children
’
s Hospital in
Calgary on July 13, 2002 and moved to Edmonton where she became a patient at
the Cross Cancer Institute. She died on September 5, 2002.

[
3
]

After Lawrence Hughes
’
consent to the blood transfusions, a schism developed
in the Hughes family and between Mr. Hughes and the Watch Tower Bible and Tract
Society which oversees the Jehovah
’
s
Witness community in Canada. The marriage ended in divorce after a trial in
this court in October, 2003.

[
4
]

The litigation regarding this
young woman continues. On August 25, 2004 Lawrence Hughes was appointed
Administrator
ad litem
of the Estate of Bethany Hughes, and on the same
day this action was commenced. The Statement of Claim contains direct claims by
Lawrence Hughes and also claims under both the
Fatal Accidents Act,
RSA
2000, c. F-8 and the

Survival of Actions Act,
RSA 2000, c. S-27.

[
5
]

At the commencement of this application,
Mr. Hughes discontinued the action against Arliss Hughes. The remaining
defendants fall into three groups: Merrill Morrell, Thomm Bokor and the Watch
Tower Bible and Tract Society (
“
the Watch Tower
Defendants
”
), Shane Heath Brady and David Miles Gnam (
“
the Watch Tower Lawyers
”
) and Dr. Robert Turner, Dr. Andrew Belch, various John and Jane Does, Cross
Cancer Institute, and Alberta Cancer Board (the
“
Health Care Defendants
”
). Her Majesty
the Queen in Right of Alberta is both a plaintiff and defendant.

[
6
]

The applications to strike the
Statement of Claim are brought by the Watch Tower Defendants and the Watch
Tower Lawyers. While there is no application by the Health Care Defendants, the
other defendants request that the court strike the action against all of the
defendants.

[
7
]

The Statement of Claim was issued
by Mr. Marshall, a lawyer. However, when these applications were heard, Mr.
Hughes represented himself. At the beginning of the hearing, I granted Mr.
Marshall
’
s application to make both oral and written
submissions. I concluded that this was warranted because some of the defendants
seek costs against Mr. Marshall personally.

HISTORY OF THE PREVIOUS LITIGATION

The Child Welfare Proceedings

[
8
]

On February 18, 2002 the Director
of Child Welfare (
“
Director
”
)
applied for Apprehension and Medical Treatment Orders before Jordan P.C.J. The
Orders were granted after a contested hearing.

[
9
]

An appeal by Bethany and Arliss
Hughes to this court, together with applications for new evidence and for
habeas
corpus
were dismissed by Kent J. on April 10, 2002 (
B.H. (Next Friend
of ) v. Alberta (Director of Child Welfare),
[2002] A.J. No. 518
,
2002
ABQB 37
)).

[
10
]

On April 26, 2002 the Court of
Appeal
(
2002 ABCA 109
) dismissed an appeal of Kent

J.
’
s decision and
refused to grant an order referring the matter directly to the Supreme Court of
Canada. On May 6, 2002 Bethany and Arliss Hughes applied for leave to appeal to
the Supreme Court of Canada. That application was dismissed on July 11, 2002.

[
11
]

In June, 2002 the earlier orders
were set to expire. The Director applied to the Provincial Court for Temporary
Guardianship and Treatment Orders. On June 17, 2002 a hearing commenced before
Vickery P.C.J. but the number of hearing days set aside proved to be
insufficient. On June 24, 2002 the trial was adjourned to October, 2002.
Bethany thus remained a ward of the province, as she had been since the ruling
of Jordan P.C.J. on February 18, 2002.

[
12
]

On June 30, 2002 Bethany
’
s treating physicians confirmed that her AML had
relapsed. On July 2, 2002 the Director applied to Vickery P.C.J. to determine
the status of his wardship. Bethany
’
s
treating oncologist testified at the hearing. His recommendation was one of
palliative care which would not require blood transfusions. Bethany gave
evidence, as did two of her treating physicians who testified that in their
opinion Bethany met the criteria for a mature minor and was competent to make
informed decisions about her treatments. Lawrence Hughes was present and made
submissions. The Court held that there was no longer any need for state
wardship of Bethany. She was discharged from the Children
’
s Hospital on July 13, 2002.

The Divorce Proceedings

[
13
]

Lawrence Hughes commenced a
divorce action on July 25, 2002. In the divorce proceedings Mr. Hughes
continued to challenge Arliss Hughes
’

opposition to the blood transfusions. After a 4 day trial in October, 2003
Nation J. granted the divorce and determined certain issues of corollary
relief. (
Hughes v. Hughes
,
2003 Carswell Alta 1605 (Q.B.)
)

These Proceedings

[
14
]

By
ex parte
order granted
August 25, 2004 Lawrence Hughes was appointed Administrator
ad litem
of
the Estate of Bethany Hughes. An application to set aside ths appointment was
dismissed by this court on February 25, 2005 (
Hughes (Estate of) v.
Hughes,
2005 ABQB 125
).

RULE 129

[
15
]

The applications are brought
pursuant to Rule 129:

129(1)   The court may at any stage of the proceedings
order to be struck or amended any pleadings in the action, on the ground that

(a)         it discloses no cause of action or
defence, as the case may be, or

(b)        it is scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,
or

(c)         it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the
fair trial of the action, or

(d)        it is otherwise an abuse of the process of
the court,

and may
order the action to be stayed or dismissed or judgment to be entered
accordingly.

(2)        No evidence shall be admissible on an
application under clause (a) of subrule (1).

[
16
]

The defendants say that the
Statement of Claim discloses no cause of action or that because of the previous
litigation, this action is either scandalous, frivolous and vexatious or an
abuse of the court
’
s process. An application under Rule 129(1)(a) is
considered without evidence. In applications which rely on Rule 129(1)(b) and
(d), the court may consider affidavit evidence. Arliss and Lawrence

Hughes
each swore lengthy affidavits. The defendants brought a preliminary application
to strike portions of Lawrence Hughes
’

affidavits. Given my conclusions, even where they invoke Rule 129(1)(b) and
(d), it is not necessary to rule on the affidavits.

Rule 129(1)(a)

[
17
]

The test under Rule 129(1)(a) was
set out by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Hunt v. T & N, PLC et al
,

1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
,
[1990] 2 S.C.R 959
at para
33
:

…
assuming
that the facts as stated in the statement of claim can be proved, is it
"plain and obvious" that the plaintiff's statement of claim discloses
no reasonable cause of action?

As in
England, if there is a chance that the plaintiff might succeed, then the
plaintiff should not be "driven from the judgment seat." Neither the
length and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the cause of action, nor
the potential for the defendant to present a strong defence should prevent the
plaintiff from proceeding with his or her case.

Only if the action is certain to fail because it contains a radical
defect
…
should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's
statement of claim be struck out
…

[
18
]

In
Tottrup v. Alberta
(Minister of Environmental Protection)
(2000),
2000 ABCA 121 (CanLII)
,
81 Alta. L.R. (3d) 27
,

[2000] A.J. No. 435
Conrad J.A., for the majority, made the following comments
regarding Rule 129(1)(a) at paras. 7, 9, and 12:

7.          Under Rule 129(1)(a) neither the plaintiff
nor the defendant is entitled to rely on affidavit evidence. If a plaintiff has
not alleged facts capable of supporting a cause of action, then a defendant
ought not be put to the time, expense and consequences of further litigation.
Conversely, if it is not plain and obvious that no cause of action exists, an
application to strike must fail.

9.          Although the pleadings should be liberally
interpreted, the Court has a duty to apply the Rule as it is intended. If the
alleged facts, examined in light of the existing law, do not disclose a cause
of action the claim should be struck. Needless litigation should be avoided.

12.        There is no need to wait for an application
for summary judgment. An application for summary judgment requires sworn
evidence. Frequently, it involves extensive affidavits and cross-examinations.
For the purposes of a R. 129(1)(a) application there is no need (in fact no
opportunity) for sworn evidence. The plaintiff
receives the benefit of an
assumption that all the facts which he or she has chosen to plead are true
.
It is not necessary to wait for summary judgment to evaluate whether those
facts, interpreted in light of the existing law, establish a cause of action.

Rule 129(1)(b) and (d)

[
19
]

In
Decock v. Alberta
(2000),

2000 ABCA 122 (CanLII)
,
255 A.R. 234 (C.A.)
, leave to appeal allowed
(2000),
293 A.R. 388 (note)

(S.C.C.)
(Notice of discontinuance filed September 10, 2001
)
Russell
J.A. said at p. 257:

It is
difficult to conceive of a claim which discloses a cause of action and which
could be considered scandalous, frivolous, embarrassing or an abuse of process
.

Despite this comment, the
Rule exists and courts have used it to strike out pleadings.
In
Dykun v.
Odishaw
(2000),
2000 ABQB 548 (CanLII)
,
267 A.R.

318 (Q.B.)
this court adopted the
following passage from the Ontario High Court in
Lang Michener and
Fabian, Re
(1987),
1987 CanLII 172 (ON HCJ)
,
37 D.L.R. (4
th
) 685
at 691
:

...a
proceeding is vexatious if it satisfies any of the following tests:

(a)
the
bringing of one or more actions to determine an issue which has already been
determined by a court of competent jurisdiction constitutes a vexatious
proceeding;

(b)
where it is obvious that an action cannot
succeed, or if the action would lead to no possible good, or if no reasonable
person can reasonably expect to obtain relief, the action is vexatious;

(c)
vexatious actions include those brought
for an improper purpose, including the harassment and oppression of other
parties by multifarious proceedings brought for purposes other than the
assertion of legitimate rights;

(d)
it is a general characteristic of
vexatious proceedings that grounds and issues raised tend to be rolled forward
into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with actions
brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant in
earlier proceedings;

(e)
in determining whether proceedings are
vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of the matter and not just
whether there was originally a good cause of action;

(f)
the failure of the person instituting the
proceedings to pay the costs of unsuccessful proceedings is one factor to be
considered in determining whether proceedings are vexatious;

(g)
the respondent's conduct in persistently
taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial decisions can be considered vexatious
conduct of legal proceedings.

[
20
]

While often an action is
determined to be an abuse of the court
’
s
process when it is
res

judicata,
there are other
instances in which such a finding may be made. For example, where the plaintiff
has an ulterior motive or seeks a collateral advantage, where a second action
is commenced while a first action still exists, or where there is issue
estoppel. I agree with the following observation of this court in
J.A.
Industries (Canada) Ltd. v. Highfield Development Ltd.
(1998),
1998 ABQB 817 (CanLII)
,
67 Alta.
L.R. (3d) 349 (Master)
at 360
:

Abuse of
process is not a closed category:
Hurley v. Co-operators General
Insurance Co.
,
1998 NSCA 127 (CanLII)
,
160 D.L.R. (4th) 645 (N.S.C.A.)
. There the Court says,
pp.

658‑59:

For the
purpose of this appeal, it is neither necessary, nor desirable, to define, or
to limit, the phrase "abuse of the process of the court", as that
phrase is used in Civil Procedure Rule 14.25. It is sufficient to note, only,
that the phrase, in the context of rule 14.25, contemplates that, in
commencing, or maintaining, a legal proceeding, the process of the court is
being misused, or is being used for an improper purpose; as opposed to an
action being brought, or maintained, for the assertion of legitimate rights.

THE STATEMENT OF CLAIM

[
21
]

The Statement of Claim is twenty
one pages (forty five paragraphs). Our system of pleading and indeed Rule
129(1)(a) require that the Statement of Claim disclose a cause of action. A
cause of action has been defined as
“
a
set of facts, which, if established, would entitle the plaintiff to some form
of relief.
”
(See
Scotia Mortgage Corp. v. Goss

(1987),
1987 CanLII 3510 (AB QB)
,
83 A.R. 15 (Q.B.)
). Traditionally we categorize causes of action into
areas of law -- tort, contract, property, etc. As I read the Statement of
Claim, all of the Plaintiffs
’
claims are in
tort, with the possible exception of one which may also claim for breach of
fiduciary duty. The theory of the plaintiffs
’

case as described by Mr. Marshall during argument is that the Health Care
Defendants did not obtain free and informed consent from Bethany Hughes while she
was in their care. Her consent was invalid and uninformed because of the
influence exercised over her by the Watch Tower Defendants and the Watch Tower
Lawyers (and by her mother, Arliss Hughes). Accordingly, the Health Care
Defendants committed a trespass against her. It is also alleged that they were
negligent in their treatment.

[
22
]

This theory is supported by the
manner in which the Statement of Claim is drafted. The crux of the pleading is
para. 27 which reads:
“
In particular, at the time of her admission to the
Defendant Cross Cancer Clinic (sic) until the time of her death, the Health
Care Defendants knew or ought to have known, and the fact is that: ...
”
This is followed by ten subparagraphs which describe
the conduct of Arliss Hughes, the Watch Tower Defendants and the Watch Tower
Lawyers. These are presumably the particulars as to why Bethany Hughes
’
consent was invalid. If the true target of this
lawsuit were the Health Care Defendants, these 10
“
particulars
”

could be treated as particulars of the trespass or negligence of the Health
Care Defendants, without adding the others defendants as parties. However, as
borne out by Mr. Hughes
’
brief and the submissions made at the hearing, one of
the aims of the lawsuit is to challenge the beliefs and practices of the Watch
Tower Bible and Tract Society of Canada. The Statement of Claim also alleges a
conspiracy among all of the defendants and pleads joint and several liability.

[
23
]

Because Rule 129(1)(a) requires
that the court focus on the concept of a cause of action, or causes of action,
the Watch Tower Defendants and the Watch Tower Lawyers have attempted to
distill from the Statement of Claim a number of discrete torts. Having isolated
those torts, these Defendants argue that either for policy reasons enunciated
in other cases those torts have no application to the facts alleged here, or
that in some instances the law does not recognize the tort alleged. Further,
they argue that the Statement of Claim does not allege particulars as required
by the Rules.

CLAIMS ON BEHALF OF BETHANY HUGHES

Claims against the Watch Tower Defendants

1.       Undue Influence

[
24
]

The Statement of Claim pleads that
the Watch Tower Defendants (together with Arliss Hughes)
“
imposed their influence on Bethany in order to
dissuade her from questioning her belief system which informed her belief that
it was against God
’
s law to take a blood transfusion, and that if she
did, that she would perish in Armageddon and be eternally damned. In the
premises, these Defendants exerted undue influence on Bethany
”
(Statement of Claim - paras. 20 and 27(b)). Further,
these Defendants

(together with Arliss Hughes)
“
all overtly influenced Bethany to believe that blood
transfusions were wrong and would not help cure her cancer and intentionally
misstated to Bethany that a chemotherapy/blood transfusion protocol for her
leukemia was experimental when it was not
”

(Statement of Claim para. 27(a)).
“
In
the premises, The Watch Tower Defendants committed the torts of deceit and
undue influence, all of which contributed to and led to the circumstances
causing the death of Bethany
”
(Statement of
Claim para. 44).

[
25
]

The applicants submit that the
tort of undue influence does not exist in Canadian law.
In
Khaper v.
Canada
(1999),
1999 CanLII 8914 (FC)
,
178 F.T.R. 68 (T.D.)
the plaintiff alleged that he was
pressured into signing a resignation from the RCMP while he was under mental
disability and undergoing psychiatric treatment. The statement of claim alleged
that the Crown was liable in tort for
“
undue
influence.
”
The defendant submitted that breach of the equitable
principle of undue influence did not trigger any right or relief against the
Crown under the
Crown Liability Act
because undue influence,
per se,

is not a recognized tort. The court stated at para 15:
“
Certainly Canadian law has yet no separate tort of
undue influence.
”

[
26
]

Mr. Hughes submits that such a
tort is recognized in the United States and ought to be recognized in Canada;
that a statement of claim which pleads a novel cause of action ought not to be
struck. He relies on the decision of the California Appellate Court in
Wollersheim
v. Church of Scientology
(1989), 212 Cal. App. 3d 872. In that case the
court found the Church of Scientology liable for the tort of intentional
infliction of emotional distress. Although the court discusses coercion of Mr.
Wollersheim in the context of whether as a fact he voluntarily participated in
the church
’
s activities and in the context of whether the church
was entitled to constitutional protection, undue influence was not discussed as
a cause of action.

[
27
]

It appears that other American
courts do not recognize such a tort. In
Bragdon v. Twenty‑Five
Twelve Assocs. Ltd. P
’
ship
856
A.2d 1165
the Court of Appeal for the District of Columbia said,
“
there is no tort of undue influence, and there is no
right to damages, as distinct from restitution, because of such influence
”
(at p. 1173). In
Umstead v. Umstead
2004
U.S. Dist. Lexis 27179 the Court for the District of Rhode Island stated that
“
this court finds more persuasive the opinions which
hold that undue influence is not a tort, but rather a set of circumstances
which give rise to an equitable remedy such as rescission.
”
(at p. 8)

[
28
]

I agree with the conclusion of
both
Khaper
and
Umstead
that undue influence is not
a separate tort for which there is a remedy in damages and accordingly, these
allegations do not disclose a cause of action and ought to be struck.

2.       Misrepresentation and Deceit

[
29
]

I interpret para. 27(a) that the
defendants
“
intentionally misstated to Bethany that a
chemotherapy/blood transfusion treatment protocol for her leukemia was
experimental when in fact it was not
”
as
a claim for fraudulent misrepresentation, also known as deceit. There are no
particulars pleaded as required by Rule 115. The elements of the tort are described
in Klar, L.N,
“
Tort Law
”

(Carswell, Second Edition) at p.490:

To
succeed in deceit, a plaintiff must prove that (1) a false representation or
statement was made by the defendant, (2) which was knowingly false, (3) was
made with the intention to deceive the plaintiff, and (4) which materially
induced the plaintiff to act, resulting in damage.

[
30
]

In his brief, Mr. Hughes submits
that
“
the Society
’
s
teachings and publications and its misquotations serve to render a follower
’
s mind closed to outside information
”
and that
“
one
could suppose that Doctors talking with Jehovah
’
s Witness patients often feel helpless and are unable to convey
realistic levels of success of bloodless techniques
”
(Plaintiffs
’

brief para. 59). As I understand the pleading, it is that the Watch Tower Society
’
s belief in the abstention from blood transfusions is
a part of an
“
indoctrination process
”
that misrepresents the benefits of blood transfusions during cancer
treatment. In other words, the religious doctrine of the Jehovah
’
s Witness faith leads one away from scientific truth.

[
31
]

The Watch Tower Defendants
submit that this line of argument is not justiciable.
In
Syndicat v.
Amselem,
[2004] 2 S.C.R. 551
,
2004 SCC 47
Amselem, an Orthodox Jew,
built a succah (a small enclosed temporary hut) on his balcony in order to
comply with the commandment mandated by the Bible for the festival of Succot.
The syndicate of co-owners applied for an injunction preventing Amselem and
others from putting up a succah on their balconies as it violated a by-law
which prohibited decorations, alterations and constructions on the balconies.
The injunction was granted and an appeal to the Quebec Court of Appeal
dismissed. The Supreme Court of Canada allowed the appeal. At issue was whether
the by-law infringed the appellants
’

freedom of religion protected under the Quebec
Charter.

[
32
]

Justice Iacobucci for the majority
began his analysis by citing the decision of Dickson J. (as he then was) in
R.
v. Big M. Drug Mart
,
[1990] 1 S.C.R. at 94
, 95 and 135:

A truly
free society is one which can accommodate a wide variety of beliefs, diversity
of tastes and pursuits, customs and codes of conduct
…
The essence of the concept of freedom of religion is
the right to entertain such religious beliefs as a person chooses, the right to
declare religious beliefs openly and without fear of hindrance or reprisal, and
the right to manifest religious belief by worship and practice or by teaching
and dissemination.

But the concept means more than that.

…

Freedom
means that
…
no one is to be forced to act in a way contrary to his
beliefs or his conscience.

…

With the

Charter
, it has become the right of every Canadian to work out for himself
or herself what his or her religious obligations, if any, should be and it is
not for the state to dictate otherwise (at para: 40
Amselem
).

[
33
]

Justice Iacobucci concluded at
paras. 50 and 51:

…
the
State is in no position to be, nor should it become, the arbiter of religious
dogma. Accordingly, courts should avoid judicially interpreting and thus
determining, either explicitly or implicitly, the content of a subjective
understanding of religious requirement, "obligation", precept,
"commandment", custom or ritual. Secular judicial determinations of
theological or religious disputes, or of contentious matters of religious
doctrine, unjustifiably entangle the court in the affairs of religion.

That said,
while a court is not qualified to rule on the validity or veracity of any given
religious practice or belief, or to choose among various interpretations of
belief, it is qualified to inquire into the sincerity of a claimant
’
s belief, where sincerity is in fact at issue: see
Jones
,

Attis v. New Brunswick District No. 15 Board of Education.
It is
important to emphasize, however, that the sincerity of belief simply implies an
honesty of belief: see
Thamas v. Indiana Employment Review Board.

(Cites omitted)

[
34
]

While the

Charter
does not
form a part of this case yet, the observations of Iacobucci J. are equally
applicable here. The Statement of Claim does not challenge the sincerity of
Bethany
’
s belief. It challenges the religious doctrine of the
Jehovah
’
s Witness faith.
According to

Amselem

this would require the court to become the arbiter of religious dogma.

[
35
]

Lawrence Hughes submits that
freedom of religion is not absolute. He relies on two cases. In
Victoria
Boer v. Watch Tower Bible and Tract of Canada et al

(2003),
2003 CanLII 2429 (ON SC)
,
65 O.R.(3d)
343 (Ont. S.C.)
Victoria Boer, who was raised as a Jehovah
’
s Witness, was sexually molested by her father during
her childhood. At the age of 19, she disclosed the abuse to L, a church elder.
L advised her that in accordance with the Bible she should confront her father
in front of elders and give him a chance to repent. Victoria agreed and a
meeting was held with church elders B and C as well as Victoria
’
s father. Subsequently, the facts of the meeting
leaked out into the community and no sanctions were imposed on her father.
Victoria felt ostracized by the community and found having to describe the
sexual abuse in detail in front of her father and the church elders to be
traumatic.

[
36
]

Victoria alleged that B and C
acted negligently and in breach of a fiduciary duty owed to her. B and C argued
that their actions were protected by their right to freedom of religion under
the
Charter
. In attempting to balance these claims, Molloy J. held at
paras. 132, 133 and 139:

I accept
the defendant's position that protection of freedom of religion is an important
factor to be considered in this case. I also accept that the courts should
generally be reluctant to intervene in matters which are purely spiritual,
particularly involving the discipline by the church of one of its members.
Traditionally, courts have refused to allow their process to be used for the
enforcement of a purely ecclesiastical decree or order, exercising civil
jurisdiction only where some property or civil right is affected thereby.

…

However,
Canadian courts have held that freedom of religion is not absolute. Where the
exercise of religious beliefs adversely affects the rights of others, the
courts can and will intervene.

…

…
a
tort committed by a person in the course of what he or she sincerely believes
to be a religious duty is not automatically shielded from scrutiny by the
courts by operation of the constitutional protection for freedom of religion.
Where the rights of an individual are in conflict with the religious freedom
rights of another, the courts can, and will, balance the competing rights in
considering what, if any, remedy is appropriate.

[
37
]

Molloy J. held B and C liable for
all of Victoria
’
s claims against them. It seems to me that the
Boer

case involved the manner in which Ms. Boer was treated by members of her
church, both as regards to the assault by her father and the humiliation
involved in then publicly disclosing this to the elders. No similar allegation
is raised in this case. There is nothing in the pleading which alleges that
Bethany Hughes was mistreated by members of the Church. Rather, Mr. Hughes
challenges the beliefs of the Jehovah
’
s
Witness faith by alleging that the defendants misrepresented scientific fact.

[
38
]

Molko v. Holy Spirit
Association for the Unification of World Christianity
(1988) 46
Cal.3d.1092 (Supreme Court of California) is one of the so called brainwashing
cases. Molko was recruited into the Unification Church. He alleged that the
church had used deception and fraud to seduce him into the church. He sued,
alleging fraud, intentional infliction of emotional distress, false
imprisonment and restitution. The church conceded that it had knowingly
misrepresented its identity with the intent to induce Molko to firstly
associate with the recruiters and later to join the church
’
s activities. The California Court of Appeal granted
summary judgment in favour of the Church. The Supreme Court of California
allowed the appeal except on the issue of false imprisonment. The court
concluded that there were issues to be tried with respect to the church
’
s conduct. It disagreed with the Court of Appeal
’
s conclusion that consideration of the fraud claims
would require questioning the authenticity and force of the church
’
s teachings (i.e. the forbidden inquiry). Rather, the
Supreme Court was of the view that the challenge was not to the teachings but
to the church
’
s practice of misrepresenting or concealing its
identity in order to bring unsuspecting outsiders into its environment.

[
39
]

I find the nature of the
allegations in
Molko
to be distinguishable. The Unification
Church was found to have engaged in fraud to solicit new members. The fraud was
the failure to reveal the church
’
s
true plans, a fact deliberately concealed from the plaintiff. The alleged fraud
was not an inquiry into the beliefs of the church, but rather as to their
practices in recruiting new members.

[
40
]

Here, the crux of the Statement of
Claim is that the beliefs of the Jehovah
’
s
Witness regarding blood transfusions are wrong and contrary to scientific
knowledge. This is the very inquiry that Iacobucci J. warns the court not to
pursue. Mr. Hughes asks this court to interpret the content of a religious
precept. This request is not justiciable and those portions of the Statement of
Claim which raise those allegations are struck.

[
41
]

The Statement of Claim also
describes certain acts of Arliss Hughes and the Watch Tower Defendants which
occurred while Bethany was still alive and a patient in the Children
’
s Hospital. For example at para. 19 it is alleged that
these defendants influenced Bethany to believe that blood transfusions were
wrong and that she should resist such treatment. The paragraph concludes that:
“
these Defendants misled Bethany by intentionally
misstating to her that her treatment protocol was experimental when in fact it
was not.
”
I note that there are no particulars of this
misstatement as required by Rule 115. Further, it is clear from the Statement
of Claim that Bethany had the chemotherapy treatment including blood
transfusions despite her protestations. It is difficult to see how she relied
upon these representations to her detriment, an aspect that must be present for
the tort of misrepresentation to occur. I fail to see a cause of action as it
relates to the alleged conduct of these defendants in the hospital. If these
allegations are related to the larger allegations of misrepresentation as to
the Jehovah
’
s Witness faith, then they ought to be struck for the

[
42
]

There are allegations about the
conduct of Arliss
Hughes
in the hospital (para.
27
(f)) which given the

,
1983 CanLII 21 (SCC)
,
[1983] 1 S.C.R. 205
, there is no separate tort
of breach of statutory duty, unless the legislation creates such a remedy. This
decision was re
affirmed in
Frame v. Smith
,
1987 CanLII 74 (SCC)
,
[1987] 2 S.C.R. 99
(at
para.
82
) and followed by our Court of Appeal
in

Tottrup
(at

). The

Claim of Conspiracy
Against All of the Defendants

[
57
]

Mr. Hughes claims that all the
defendants committed the tort of conspiracy against Bethany when they
“
combined together and actively took part in the
planning, execution furtherance, and performance of wrongful acts which were
done for the predominant purpose of insuring that Bethany received the
alternative treatment from the Health Care Defendants
”
and that resulted in her death (para. 41).

[
58
]

On its face this pleading sets out
the elements of a cause of action. While the applicants submit that a plea of
conspiracy must allege that the predominant purpose of the conspiracy requires
the intent to injure (and this has not been pleaded), the law in Canada is
otherwise. In
Hunt v. T & N plc,
Wilson J. wrote
“
an actionable conspiracy will exist if the defendants
combine to act unlawfully, their conduct is directed toward the plaintiff (or
the plaintiff and others) and the likelihood of injury to the plaintiff is
known to the defendants or should have been known to them in the circumstances
”
(at p. 340).

[
59
]

I note that the Supreme Court of
Canada has on two relatively recent occasions cautioned against the extension
of the tort of conspiracy beyond the commercial context. Estey J. in
Can.
Cement LaFarge

Ltd. v. B.C. Lightweight Aggregate Ltd.
,

1983 CanLII 23 (SCC)
,
[1983] 1 S.C.R. 452
commented at p.

473
:

The tort
of conspiracy to injure, even without the extension to include a conspiracy to
perform unlawful acts where there is a constructive intent to injure, has been
the target of much criticism throughout the common law world. It is indeed a
commercial anachronism as so aptly illustrated by Lord Diplock in
Lonrho

... In fact, the action may have lost much of its usefulness in our commercial
world, and survives in our law as an anomaly.

[
60
]

Wilson J.
in
Frame
v. Smith
, a case which I will discuss more fully later in these
reasons, refused to extend the tort to the family law context. She said at
para.19
in

Frame
:

Although

“
the law concerning the scope of the tort of conspiracy
is far from clear
”
, the criticisms which have been levelled at the tort
give good reason to pause before extending it beyond the commercial context.

[
61
]

In the context of this case which
is not a commercial case, it is important to clearly pead the particulars of
the alleged conspiracy. The Ontario Court of Appeal in
Normart Management
v. West Hill Redevelopment Co. et al
1998 CanLII 2447 (ON CA)
,
155 D.L.R. (4
th
) 627

described
a proper pleading of conspiracy at para. 21 as:

The
statement of claim should describe who the several parties are and their
relationship with each other. It should allege the agreement between the
defendants to conspire, and state precisely what the purpose or what were the
objects of the alleged conspiracy, and it must then proceed to set forth, with
clarity and precision, the overt acts which are alleged to have been done by
each of the alleged conspirators in pursuance and in furtherance of the
conspiracy; and lastly, it must allege the injury and damage occasioned to the
plaintiff thereby.

(See also
Hovsepian v.
Westfair Foods Ltd.,
2001 ABQB 700
at para.
105
)

[
62
]

The Statement of Claim does not
with clarity and precision set out the overt acts which are alleged to have
been done by each of the conspirators. Indeed the pleading of conspiracy is
very brief. I expect that if one asked for particulars, the plaintiffs would
simply repeat all of the other paragraphs in the Statement of Claim; in other
words that the particulars of the unlawful acts of this conspiracy are the
“
undue influence,
”

“
misrepresentation
”

and
“
deceit
”
previously
discussed. While a court should be slow to strike out a pleading because of
lack of particulars, to permit the plaintiffs to pursue the conspiracy plea
against the Watch Tower Defendants against whom there are no other causes of
action, is to enable the plaintiffs to litigate precisely the matters that I
have just struck out. That would be an abuse of this court
’
s process.

[
63
]

This leaves the remaining
defendants (the Watch Tower Lawyers and the Health Care Defendants). It is
important for these defendants to know the particulars of the conspiracy in
which they allegedly engaged. This is a serious allegation. Surely they are
entitled to know the precise acts in which each of them engaged and which are
alleged to constitute the conspiracy. In my view without those particulars,
there is no valid cause of action in conspiracy contained in this pleading.
Therefore the allegations of conspiracy against all defendants are struck.

PERSONALLY

[

]

It is my conclusion that all
claims advanced by Lawrence Hughes in his personal capacity should be struck.

[

Lawrence Hughes claims that the

”

[

[
67

’
s whereabouts and treatment. (Statement of Claim -
para. 40). Paragraph 43 alleges false representation by the Watch Tower
Defendants and para. 44 is a plea of deceit and undue influence.

[
68
]

The defendants submit that in
light of the Supreme Court of Canada
decision in
Frame v. Smith
,
these
types of tort claims (conspiracy, deceit and misrepresentation) ought not to be
extended to the family law context and that although Lawrence Hughes sues
defendants who are not
“
family members
”

the policy considerations enunciated
in
Frame
ought to apply
here.
In
Frame
and in the Alberta Court of Appeal
decision in
Sturkenboom
v. Davies
(1997),
1996 ABCA 350 (CanLII)
,
187 A.R. 290
a non-custodial parent sued both the
custodial parent and others (
in
Frame
, a new spouse of the
custodial parent, and
in

Sturkenboom
, the custodial parent
’
s father). Both actions were brought in the context of
access to children. Both actions included pleas in tort -
in

Frame
,
wilful
infliction of harm, intentional interference with a legal right, and conspiracy
and
in

Sturkenboom
, conspiracy, interference with the
parent/child relationship, fraudulent misrepresentation, negligent
misrepresentation, and intentional infliction of mental suffering.

[
69
]

The policy reasons for refusing to
extend tort law to the family context are discussed at length in the minority
judgment of Wilson J.
in

Frame
.
La Forest J. for the majority
approved and summarized those reasons at para.76:

The
husband in the present case also sought to rely on the tort of conspiracy but
as my colleague Wilson J. explains in her judgment, there are grave
disadvantages associated with applying this tort to circumstances like the
present. Further, as she notes, this court has made it clear that it does not
look kindly upon the extension of this tort, which it regards as an anomaly.

[
70
]

Further, at para. 77 the court
refused to consider creating a new tort:

It
would, of course, be possible for the courts to devise a new tort to meet the
situation. And the temptation to do so is clearly present, for one cannot help
but feel sympathy for the appellant and others in like situations. But there
are formidable arguments against the creation of such a remedy. I have already
mentioned the undesirability of provoking suits within the family circle. The
spectacle of parents not only suing their former spouses but also the
grandparents, and aunts and uncles of their children, to say nothing of close
family friends, for interfering with rights of access is one that invites one
to pause. The disruption of the familial and social environment so important to
a child's welfare may well have been considered reason enough for the law's
inaction, though there are others.

[
71
]

McFayden J.A.
in
Sturkenboom

observed at paras.
17 and 18
that:

The comments
in
Frame v. Smith
and the Court's overriding concern for the best
interests of the children of a relationship militate against any extension of
the actions of fraudulent or negligent misrepresentation and other similar tort
actions to the family situation which concerns us here. The reasoning which
makes it undesirable to permit parties involved in custody and access disputes
to bring actions based on the torts of conspiracy and intentional infliction of
harm applies with equal force to other tort actions.

The
Supreme Court of Canada found that torts based on parental rights to children,
whether styled as interference with the parent/child relationship, or
enticement, harbouring, seduction or loss of services, were not available in
Canada to enforce access rights.

[
72
]

She concluded at para 24:

In my
view, the decision of
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Frame v. Smith

is not distinguishable. It applies in Alberta and applies to the circumstances
of this case. The tort of interference with the parent/child relationship, in
any of its forms, including those of harbouring and enticing the child, is not
available in the circumstances of a domestic dispute involving issues of
custody and access to children, either in an action against the parent or in an
action against members of the parent's family or friends who assist the parent.

[
73
]

Is there any valid reason not to
reach the same conclusion in this case? Technically, Mr. Hughes
’
claim is not one of access, because he can no longer
have access to Bethany. Accordingly, continued litigation that might affect the
best interest of the child is no longer a consideration. Also, it might be
argued that as the action has been discontinued against Arliss Hughes, this is
no longer a claim in the family context. The Statement of Claim is pleaded as a
failure by the defendants to provide Mr. Hughes with the information regarding
Bethany
’
s whereabouts or treatment, and a conspiracy to keep
her whereabouts and treatment protocol from him. Mr. Hughes submits that all of
these reasons ought to distinguish this claim from the pleadings
considered in
Frame

and
in
Sturkenboom
.

[
74
]

The claims assume that the
defendants had a duty to provide Mr. Hughes with the information. Presumably,
it is Mr. Hughes
’
intention to establish that his relationships with
the Watch Tower Defendants and with the Health Care Defendants are sufficient
to give rise to a duty of care. For the purposes of this application I have
assumed that these duties of care exist. Is this claim, which includes many
repetitions of various torts anything other than a claim in tort for access,
including access to information about a child? In my view it is not. It has
been dressed up as something else but in essence Mr. Hughes wants damages
because he alleges that he was denied access to Bethany and to information
about her treatment. He pleads that had he had the information, he would have
contacted the Director. Lawrence Hughes
’

claims against the defendants are precisely the types of claims that ought not
to be recognized as causes of action for the reasons given by
the Supreme Court
of Canada in
Frame
.

[
75
]

Even if I am incorrect in this
conclusion, I am prepared to find that Mr. Hughes
’
claims are an abuse of this court
’
s
process. In an application which invokes Rule 129(1)(d) there is no assumption
that the facts as pleaded are true. (
See
Boudreault v. Barrett
(1995),

1995 ABCA 311 (CanLII)
,
33 Alta. L.R. (3d) 60
at 65
.) Indeed, in this case the court record contradicts
the Statement of Claim.

[
76
]

The appropriate manner in which to
address his concerns at the time was to seek access as provided by the
Divorce
Act
.
Mr. Hughes did this. In the context of the divorce action Mr. Hughes
brought an application for custody of Bethany and for disclosure of her
whereabouts. On August 11, 2002 counsel for Arliss Hughes disclosed to Lawrence
Hughes Bethany
’
s location and treatment protocol. Mr. Hughes
’
application was then adjourned
sine die.
In
other words, he pursued a remedy, then chose to abandon it. When I look at the
whole history of the proceedings, I find that to advance these claims now
against any of the defendants is vexatious and an abuse of the court
’
s process. It is an attempt to litigate that which was
not pursued in the summer of 2002. Accordingly Mr. Hughes
’
claims against the various defendants for deceit,
conspiracy and misrepresentation are struck.

Claims Against the Watch Tower Lawyers

[
77
]

It is unclear whether the
Statement of Claim pleads a cause of action by Lawrence Hughes against the
Watch Tower Lawyers. Paragraphs 27(i) and (j) make allegations against the
lawyers. I earlier found that any solicitor client relationship was between
Bethany and/or Arliss Hughes and the lawyers. The lawyers owed no duty to
Lawrence Hughes. There is no plea of a retainer between them. A lawyer does not
owe a duty to an opposing party. Indeed, in
Rondel v. Worsley,
[1967]
3 All ER. 993
,
[1969] 1 AC 191
the House of Lords concluded:

I would
go rather further and say that, in context of
“
hostile litigation
”
, public policy
will usually require that a solicitor be protected from a claim in negligence
by his client
’
s opponent, since such claims could be used as a basis
for endless relitigation of disputes.

(
See also
J.A.
Industries (Canada) Ltd. v.

Highfield Development Ltd.
)

Accordingly, any claim by Lawrence Hughes in his personal capacity against the
lawyers is struck.

CONCLUSION

[
78
]

With one minor exception to which
I will refer shortly, all claims against the Watch Tower Bible and Tract
Society, Merrill Morrell and Thomm Bokor are struck. All claims by Lawrence
Hughes in his personal capacity are struck. The only remaining claims are those
brought on behalf of Bethany Hughes against the Health Care Defendants in the
torts of trespass and negligence and against David Gnam and Shane Heath Brady
in negligence or breach of fiduciary duty. All other claims on behalf of
Bethany Hughes are struck. The Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society remains a
defendant solely with respect to any vicarious liability on account of the action
against Messrs. Gnam and Brady.

[
79
]

I have tried to enumerate the
paragraphs of the Statement of Claim that should be struck. I believe them to
be paras. 10, 11, 15, 16, 19, 20, 21, 22, 25, 26 (reference to the Watch Tower
Defendants), 27(a), 27(b), 27(c), 27(d), 27(e), 27(f), 27(g), 27(h), 27(i),
29(a), 29(b), 29(c), 38, 40, 41, 42, 43, and 44.

[
80
]

Subject to submissions from
counsel, given that there has been divided success on these applications, it is
my direction that the parties should bear their owns costs. If counsel wish to
make submissions regarding costs, they are invited to contact the court to
arrange to do so.
